Wednesday ✅. Late breaking news today: Anthropic is pricing its IPO at $83. More below.

Today's newsletter is 945 words, a 3.5-minute read.

📉 The dashboard: The S&P 500 closed down 0.2%, its fifth straight losing session.

🔥 Today's stock spotlight: Take-Two Interactive Software (+6.2%) jumped ahead of tonight's release of Grand Theft Auto VI. (See below 👇)
 
 
1 big thing: ANT marching
 

Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios
 

Just when Nvidia finally got some good news, the stock has another overhang — one of its biggest customers is getting all of the attention.

Why it matters: Nvidia delivered a blockbuster earnings report after-hours yesterday, but the stock fell again today as the chip giant continues to grapple with the fallout from the Jensen Huang scandal.

🔁 The big picture: On the eve of Anthropic's long-awaited IPO, the AI trade may be focused on a shiny new opportunity.

  • Call it a classic rotation trade, as investors exchange the cloud of uncertainty surrounding Nvidia's leadership for the hope of explosive growth at the first major pure-play AI model developer to trade on public markets.
  • Nvidia got at least nine buy-to-hold downgrades from analysts after the earnings report, despite the significant revenue and earnings beat — and despite the raised outlook for the next fiscal year.

🗣️ What they're saying: Despite interim CEO Colette Kress' "assurances that growth will accelerate, Nvidia shares are down this morning as investors remain skeptical," Lauren Cassidy, chief investment officer at Founder ETFs, tells me. "Jensen's sudden departure left shareholders with more questions than answers."

Against that backdrop, the purity of the Anthropic play looks more enticing to some investors.

  • Quite simply, there's only so much capital to go around — and right now, investors might be keeping their powder dry so they can dive into Anthropic tomorrow.

🏷️ What's next: Anthropic just priced its IPO at $83 a share, well above its $70 to $78 range.

  • How it trades tomorrow — on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT — could have a big impact on the broader AI trade.

The bottom line: For now, the trade could be stuck on a giant ANT hill.

 
 
2. Back on Target 🎯
 

People at a Target store in Times Square in New York City. Photo: Craig T Fruchtman/Getty Images
 

Target is regaining traction after a prolonged slump, as its investments in food, beauty and fun items begin to pay off.

📈 Zoom in: Shares rose 4% today after the big-box retailer posted comparable sales growth of 5.6% in the quarter ended Oct. 31 — including a 5% boost in traffic — and raised its profit guidance.

  • That broke down as 4.6% growth at comparable physical stores and a digital comparable sales jump of 9.8%.

Overall, the company's revenue rose 7.1% to $27.1 billion, beating S&P Capital IQ expectations of $26.5 billion.

  • Net earnings soared 75.8% to $1.21 billion, topping expectations of $938 million.

🎯 The big picture: Target has been struggling to find its way amid runaway inflation and rapidly evolving fashion trends, but a new CEO and investments in key categories are paying off.

  • The retailer has revamped its grocery aisle presentation and food products, made significant changes to its home furnishings, and built momentum from partnerships with brands like LoveShackFancy, Pokémon and Hollister.

Go deeper: Target's turnaround accelerates

What to watch: Walmart reports earnings tomorrow morning, offering one of the most important barometers of the American consumer heading into the holiday shopping season.

4. 🕔 After hours: The GTA productivity dip
 

A screenshot of Grand Theft Auto VI featuring the game's main characters, Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval. Photo: Courtesy of Rockstar Games
 

Grand Theft Auto VI is going live at midnight, and the madness may be unlike anything we've seen before, Axios' Herb Scribner writes.

Why it matters: GTA VI has been in development for roughly 13 years and is shaping up to be the biggest cultural phenomenon of 2026. Millions of Americans are thinking about skipping work to play it.

  • The Take-Two Interactive-owned Rockstar Games release has already netted nearly $1.5 billion in sales, according to Sensor Tower estimates, with nearly 15 million digital pre-order copies sold across Xbox and PlayStation devices.

🔫 The big picture: Grand Theft Auto lets players roam a fictional city, steal cars and cause chaos — a satire of modern American life. Since debuting in 1997, it's become one of the world's biggest entertainment franchises.

  • Past editions have been set in cities modeled on Los Angeles, New York and Miami. This version returns to Miami — named Vice City in the game.
  • The last installment, Grand Theft Auto V, came out in 2013 and made $1 billion in three days, faster than any movie or game before it. More than a decade later, people are still playing it.

🍿 What they're saying: "If you took the Super Bowl, a blockbuster movie premiere and Christmas morning and rolled them all up into one, this is what you get," Justin Kenna, CEO of entertainment and tech company GameSquare, tells Axios.

  • "Even people who don't play video games know about it because it's become such a massive cultural phenomenon."

🛜 What to watch: The debut is expected to be so big that internet providers are already sounding the alarm about global bandwidth and traffic disruptions as fans begin pre-downloads, Axios' Sara Fischer writes.
